We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}2v,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2u & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2v & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2v & 1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2u & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2v,\hspace{0.222em}-2u,\hspace{0.222em}4uv⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf r (u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,\textrm d S = \iint\limits_D  \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u, \: v, \: 1 - u - v \right\rangle.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(1-u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(1-u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩,\end{aligned}

and its magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\text{ }\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot 2\cdot 3 \\  & =6\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 1,\,2u,\,v\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 1,\,1,\,u\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & 2u & v \\ 1 & 1 & u\end{vmatrix}.

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_1&=(2u)u-v\cdot1=2u^2-v,\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_2&=-(1\cdot u-v\cdot1)=v-u,\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_3&=1\cdot1-(2u)1=1-2u.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\langle 2u^2-v,\,v-u,\,1-2u\rangle.
$$

Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle u+v,\,uv,\,u\sin(uv)\rangle.
$$

For a parametrization $\mathbf r(u,v)$, the fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Differentiate with respect to one parameter while holding the other fixed.

The third coordinate requires the product rule when differentiating with respect to $u$, and the chain rule for $\sin(uv)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\bigl(u\sin(uv)\bigr)&=\sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv),\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\bigl(u\sin(uv)\bigr)&=u^2\cos(uv).\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\langle 1,\,v,\,\sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv)\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 1,\,u,\,u^2\cos(uv)\rangle.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ 1 & v & \sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv) \\ 1 & u & u^2\cos(uv)\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Expand and simplify one component at a time:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_1&=u^2v\cos(uv)-u\bigl(\sin(uv)+uv\cos(uv)\bigr)\\&=-u\sin(uv),\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_2&=-\bigl(u^2\cos(uv)-\sin(uv)-uv\cos(uv)\bigr)\\&=\sin(uv)+u(v-u)\cos(uv),\\(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_3&=1\cdot u-v\cdot1=u-v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\langle -u\sin(uv),\,\sin(uv)+u(v-u)\cos(uv),\,u-v\rangle.
$$

The first component retains the product-rule term after the two $u^2v\cos(uv)$ terms cancel.

\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle u + 2,v + 1,2 u - v - 2\rangle.
$$

For $-2\le u\le 0$ and $1\le v\le 4$.

The tangent vectors are $\mathbf r_u=\langle 1,0,2\rangle$ and $\mathbf r_v=\langle 0,1,-1\rangle$. Use

$$
A(S)=\iint_D\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,\mathrm dA.
$$

For a parametrization over $D$, use $$
A(S)=\iint_D\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,\mathrm dA
$$

Differentiate and form the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r_u&=\langle 1,0,2\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 0,1,-1\rangle,\\\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1&0&2\\0&1&-1\end{vmatrix}\\&=\langle -2,1,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|=\sqrt{(-2)^2+(1)^2+(1)^2}=\sqrt{6}.
$$

The parameter rectangle has side lengths $0-(-2)=2$ and $4-(1)=3$, so its area is $6$.

The area scale factor is constant, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(S)&=\iint_D \sqrt{6}\,\mathrm dA\\&=\sqrt{6}\cdot\operatorname{Area}(D)\\&=\sqrt{6}\cdot(6)=6 \sqrt{6}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Find the surface area of the parametric surface

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\langle u - 2,v - 2,- 2 u + 2 v\rangle.
$$

For $-1\le u\le 0$ and $1\le v\le 2$.

The tangent vectors are $\mathbf r_u=\langle 1,0,-2\rangle$ and $\mathbf r_v=\langle 0,1,2\rangle$. Use

$$
A(S)=\iint_D\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,\mathrm dA.
$$

For a parametrization over $D$, use $$
A(S)=\iint_D\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\,\mathrm dA
$$

Differentiate and form the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r_u&=\langle 1,0,-2\rangle,\\\mathbf r_v&=\langle 0,1,2\rangle,\\\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v&=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1&0&-2\\0&1&2\end{vmatrix}\\&=\langle 2,-2,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|=\sqrt{(2)^2+(-2)^2+(1)^2}=3.
$$

The parameter rectangle has side lengths $0-(-1)=1$ and $2-(1)=1$, so its area is $1$.

The area scale factor is constant, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(S)&=\iint_D 3\,\mathrm dA\\&=3\cdot\operatorname{Area}(D)\\&=3\cdot(1)=3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}- u v\\- u\\v\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- u v)&=- v\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- u)&=-1\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- u v)&=- u\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- u)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v)&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}- v\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}- u\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\- v & -1 & 0\\- u & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(-1)(1)\\&\quad -(0)(0)\\&=-1.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(- v)(1)\\&\quad +(0)(- u)\\&=v.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(- v)(0)\\&\quad -(-1)(- u)\\&=- u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\v\\- u\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}u\\2 u - e^{v}\\v\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u)&=1\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(2 u - e^{v})&=2\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(2 u - e^{v})&=- e^{v}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v)&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\- e^{v}\\1\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1 & 2 & 0\\0 & - e^{v} & 1\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(2)(1)\\&\quad -(0)(- e^{v})\\&=2.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(1)(1)\\&\quad +(0)(0)\\&=-1.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(1)(- e^{v})\\&\quad -(2)(0)\\&=- e^{v}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\- e^{v}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}- 2 u^{2} - v^{2}\\v\\u\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- 2 u^{2} - v^{2})&=- 4 u\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u)&=1\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- 2 u^{2} - v^{2})&=- 2 v\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v)&=1\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u)&=0\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}- 4 u\\0\\1\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}- 2 v\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\- 4 u & 0 & 1\\- 2 v & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(0)(0)\\&\quad -(1)(1)\\&=-1.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(- 4 u)(0)\\&\quad +(1)(- 2 v)\\&=- 2 v.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(- 4 u)(1)\\&\quad -(0)(- 2 v)\\&=- 4 u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\- 2 v\\- 4 u\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{(u )}\\\sin{(u )}\\v\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(\cos{(u )})&=- \sin{(u )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(\sin{(u )})&=\cos{(u )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(\cos{(u )})&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(\sin{(u )})&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v)&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}- \sin{(u )}\\\cos{(u )}\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\- \sin{(u )} & \cos{(u )} & 0\\0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(\cos{(u )})(1)\\&\quad -(0)(0)\\&=\cos{(u )}.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(- \sin{(u )})(1)\\&\quad +(0)(0)\\&=\sin{(u )}.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(- \sin{(u )})(0)\\&\quad -(\cos{(u )})(0)\\&=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}\cos{(u )}\\\sin{(u )}\\0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}v \cos{(u )}\\\sin{(u )}\\- v^{2}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v \cos{(u )})&=- v \sin{(u )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(\sin{(u )})&=\cos{(u )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- v^{2})&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v \cos{(u )})&=\cos{(u )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(\sin{(u )})&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- v^{2})&=- 2 v\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}- v \sin{(u )}\\\cos{(u )}\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{(u )}\\0\\- 2 v\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\- v \sin{(u )} & \cos{(u )} & 0\\\cos{(u )} & 0 & - 2 v\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(\cos{(u )})(- 2 v)\\&\quad -(0)(0)\\&=- 2 v \cos{(u )}.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(- v \sin{(u )})(- 2 v)\\&\quad +(0)(\cos{(u )})\\&=- 2 v^{2} \sin{(u )}.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(- v \sin{(u )})(0)\\&\quad -(\cos{(u )})(\cos{(u )})\\&=- \cos^{2}{(u )}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}- 2 v \cos{(u )}\\- 2 v^{2} \sin{(u )}\\- \cos^{2}{(u )}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$

Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y &=4 \\ x+2y &=16\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & =4 \\ x & =4+y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	x+2y &=16 \\
	(4+y) + 2y &=16\\
	4+3y &=16\\
	3y &=12\\
	y &=4
\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=4+y$, then we can find the value of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	x &= 4 + y \\
	   &= 4 + (4) \\
	   &=8
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 8$ and $y = 4$, which can be written as $(8, 4).$

Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2u+9v-6 &=0 \\ 2u+6v-8 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:


$$\qquad\:\:\:
\begin{cases}{\color{red}2u+9v-6=0}\hspace{2em}{\color{red}(1)} \\ {\color{blue}2u+6v-8=0}\hspace{2em}{\color{blue}(2)}\end{cases}.$$



We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $u$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	2u+6v-8 &= 0 \\
2u+6v &= 8 \\
2u &= 8 - 6v \\
u &= \dfrac{8-6v}{2} \\
u &= 4 - 3v
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $u=4-3v$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $v\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \\
	2(4-3v)+9v-6 &= 0 \\
	8-6v+9v-6 &= 0 \\
2+3v &= 0 \\
3v &= -2 \\
v &= -\dfrac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $u\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \\
	2u+9\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) -6 &= 0 \\
	2u-6-6 &= 0 \\
	2u-12 &= 0 \\
	2u &= 12 \\
	u &= 6
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=6$ and $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, which can be written as $\left(6,-\dfrac{2}{3}\right).$

\left\{\begin{aligned}-3x - 9y &=-36 \\ -7x - 4y - 1 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find the solution $(x,y)$ to this system using the method of substitution.

We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-3x - 9y &=-36 && (1) \\ -7x - 4y - 1 &=0 && (2)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(1)$, we can solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} -3x - 9y &= -36 \\ -3x &= 9y - 36 \\ x &= -3y + 12 \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=-3y + 12$ into equation $(2)$ and solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned} -7x - 4y - 1 &= 0 \\ -7\left(-3y + 12\right) - 4y - 1 &= 0 \\ 21y - 84 - 4y - 1 &= 0 \\ 17y &= 85 \\ y &= 5 \end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $y=5$ back into equation $(1)$, then we can find the value of $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned} -3x - 9\left(5\right) &= -36 \\ -3x - 45 &= -36 \\ -3x &= 9 \\ x &= -3 \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-3,\,y=5$, which can be expressed as $(-3,5)$.

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2)$, we can solve for $b$ as follows:

$$

Then, we substitute $b=2a - 3$ into equation $(1)$ and solve for $a$:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =86+11x \\ 750+7x & =86+11x \\ 750+7x-7x & =86+11x-7x \\ 750 & =86+4x \\ 750-86 & =86+4x-86 \\ 664 & =4x \\ \frac{664}{4} & =\frac{4x}{4} \\ 166 & =x \\ x & =166\end{aligned}

Calculate $$
\displaystyle\int_C \,\textrm d s,
$$ where $C$ is the arc of a semicircle of radius $4$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, as shown above.

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = L.
$$

In this case, $C$ is a semicircle of radius $r = 4.$ Its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L=\pi r=4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = 4\pi.
$$

Calculate $$
\displaystyle\int_C \,\textrm d s,
$$ where $C$ is the path shown above, traversed once counterclockwise.

The path $C$ is made up of three parts, as shown below:

![](images/f4/f4e80a23910612bd55e7578a074f23c76535139889faff479c4dd0521e7496ff.png)

Now, we make use of the following facts:

- If $C = C_1 \cup C_2 \cup C_3$ is a piecewise-smooth curve, we have

$$
\int_{C}f(x,y)\,\textrm d s =  \int_{C_1}f(x,y)\,\textrm d s + \int_{C_2}f(x,y)\,\textrm d s + \int_{C_3}f(x,y)\,\textrm d s.
$$

If $f(x,y) = x^2 + 2 y^3$ and $\mathbf r (t) = \sin t \ \mathbf i + e^{t} \ \mathbf j,$ compute $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r(t))].$

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+6{y}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x = \sin t$ and $y=e^{t}$  into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =2(\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+6({e}^{t})^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+6{e}^{2t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{sin}t\text{ }\mathbf{i}+6{e}^{2t}\text{ }\mathbf{j})\cdot (\operatorname{cos}t\text{ }\mathbf{i}+{e}^{t}\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t+6{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}2t+6{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$
If $f(x,y,z) = xz\ln{y}$ and $\mathbf r (t) =  t^2 \, \mathbf i + t  \, \mathbf j +t^3  \, \mathbf k,$ compute $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r(t))].$

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xz\operatorname{ln}y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xz\operatorname{ln}y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xz\operatorname{ln}y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =z\operatorname{ln}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{xz}{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+x\operatorname{ln}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x= t^2,$ $y = t$ and $z= t^3$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & ={t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{4}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+3{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =({t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{4}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k})\cdot (2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+3{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}) \\  & =({t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}t)\cdot 2t+({t}^{4})\cdot 1+({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}t)\cdot 3{t}^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{4}\operatorname{ln}t+{t}^{4}+3{t}^{4}\operatorname{ln}t \\  & ={t}^{4}(5\operatorname{ln}t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =(1)\,i+(2 t)\,j+(1)\,k\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((1)\,i+(1)\,j+(-2)\,k)\cdot ((1)\,i+(2 t)\,j+(1)\,k) \\  & =(1)\cdot (1)+(1)\cdot (2 t)+(-2)\cdot (1) \\  & =(1)+(2 t)+(-2) \\  & =2 t - 1.\end{aligned}

Since our circle is centered at $(0,-1)$ and has a radius of $2,$ its equation is given by

$$

Now, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$

$$

The line segment $\overline{XY}$ is a diameter of a circle. Given that $X$ and $Y$ have coordinates $(-2,4)$ and $(-6,4)$, respectively, what is the equation of the circle?

The general equation of a circle with radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ is

$$
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2.
$$

Using the distance formula to compute the distance between the points $X(-2,4)$ and $Y(-6,4),$ we find that the length of the diameter is

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{((-2)-(-6))^2+(4-4)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(4)^2+(0)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{16+0} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So the radius of the circle is

$$
r=\frac{XY}{2}=\frac{4}{2}=2.
$$

Since the center of a circle is the midpoint of the diameter, to find the center we use the midpoint formula as follows:

$$
(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\frac{y_1+y_2}{2})=(\frac{-2+(-6)}{2},\frac{4+4}{2})=(-4,4)
$$

So our circle has radius $r=2$ and center $(a,b)=(-4,4),$ and therefore it is represented by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2 & =r^2 \\ (x-(-4))^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =(2)^2 \\ (x+4)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =4\end{aligned}

Given that $λ(5a - 25b)$ and $6a - 30b$ are equal (non-zero) vectors, find the scale factor $λ$.

Notice that

$$
λ(5a - 25b)=λ(5)a+λ(-25)b.
$$

The same scale factor must multiply the whole non-zero vector. Comparing the two coefficients gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ &= \frac{6}{5} = \frac{6}{5} \\
λ &= \frac{-30}{-25} = \frac{6}{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that

$$
6a - 30b=\frac{6}{5}(5a - 25b).
$$

Therefore,

$$
λ=\frac{6}{5}
$$

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle\int\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r
$$ given that $\mathbf F(x, y) = y \,\mathbf i + (x+y)\,\mathbf j$ and $C$ is the path $\mathbf r(t) = (1+2t)\,\mathbf{i} + (1-t)\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0, 1].$

We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C\mathbf F\cdot \textrm d \mathbf r  = \int_a^b\mathbf F(\mathbf r (t))\cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,\textrm d t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x = 1 + 2t, \qquad y = 1 - t .
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =(1-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+((1+2t)+(1-t))\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =(1-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t+2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =((1-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t+2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}) \\  & =(1-t)\cdot 2+(t+2)\cdot (-1) \\  & =2-2t-t-2 \\  & =-3t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r})\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-3t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}t \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}-0 \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have that $B=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore, the period is $$
\displaystyle \frac{2\pi }{|\frac{1}{4}|}=\frac{2\pi }{\frac{1}{4}}=8\pi .
$$

$$

What is the range of the function $f(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x+\pi )-2?$

The range of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is

$$
-1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡x\le 1.
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
-1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡(4x+\pi )\le 1.
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by $-1$ and then subtracting $2$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & -1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡(4x+\pi )\le 1 \\  & 1\ge -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x+\pi )\ge -1 \\  & -1\ge \operatorname{sin}⁡(4x+\pi )-2\ge -3 \\  & -3\le f(x)\le -1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range is $f(x)\in [-3,-1].$

Find the range of the function $f(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})-3.$

$$

$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
-1\le \operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le 1.
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by $2$ and then subtracting $3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & -1\le \operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le 1 \\  & -2\le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le 2 \\  & -5\le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-\frac{\pi }{4})-3\le -1 \\  & -5\le f(x)\le -1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range is $f(x)\in [-5,-1].$

Find the equation of the midline for a transformed cosine function with a minimum value of $-13$ and a maximum value of $-1.$

A sinusoidal graph's midline (or vertical shift) is the horizontal line that divides it vertically in half. 

The equation of the midline is given by

$$
y=\frac{{y}_{\text{min}}+{y}_{\text{max}}}{2},
$$

where ${y}_{\text{min}}$ and ${y}_{\text{max}}$ are the minimum and maximum values of the function. The midline equals the average of the maximum and minimum values. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}_{\text{min}}+{y}_{\text{max}}}{2} & =\frac{-13+(-1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{-14}{2} \\  & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the midline is $y=-7.$

Calculate the period of the function

$$
f(x)=3\sin\left(\frac{\pi-2x}{3}+\frac{x}{2}\right)-4.
$$

Combine the $x$ terms inside the sine before applying the period formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\pi-2x}{3}+\frac{x}{2}
&=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{2x}{3}+\frac{x}{2}\\
&=\frac{\pi}{3}+\left(-\frac{4}{6}+\frac{3}{6}\right)x\\
&=-\frac{x}{6}+\frac{\pi}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient is $B=-\frac{1}{6}$. A negative input coefficient reverses the direction of a cycle; the period is a positive length, so use $|B|$:

$$
T=\frac{2\pi}{|B|}=\frac{2\pi}{\frac{1}{6}}=12\pi.
$$

Using only one of the two original $x$ terms would miss their combined effect. The outside factor $3$ and vertical shift $-4$ do not affect the period.

Calculate the period of the function

$$
f(x)=-2\cos\left(\frac{3x-60^{\circ}}{2}\right)+4.
$$

Angles are measured in degrees.

First rewrite the entire cosine argument to identify the coefficient of $x$:

$$
\frac{3x-60^{\circ}}{2}=\frac{3}{2}x-30^{\circ}.
$$

Thus $B=\frac{3}{2}$, rather than $3$. In degree measure the period is $T=\frac{360^{\circ}}{|B|}$, so

$$
T=\frac{360^{\circ}}{\frac{3}{2}}=360^{\circ}\cdot\frac{2}{3}=240^{\circ}.
$$

The factor $-2$ outside the cosine and the horizontal and vertical shifts do not change the period.
Find the equation of the midline for a transformed sine function with a minimum value of $-4$ and a maximum value of $8$.

The midline is the horizontal line halfway between the minimum and maximum values. Its height is their average:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \frac{y_{\text{min}}+y_{\text{max}}}{2} \\
  &= \frac{-4+8}{2} \\
  &= \frac{4}{2} \\
  &= 2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the midline is $y=2$. The quantity $\frac{8-(-4)}{2}=6$ is the amplitude, not the height of the midline.

Find the range of $f(x)=2\sin\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+1$ for all real $x$.

The sine function takes every value from $-1$ to $1$, including both endpoints. Horizontal shifts and stretches do not change this range when $x$ can be any real number. Thus,

$$
-1\le \sin\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\le 1.
$$

Multiply by $2$, then add $1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-2&\le 2\sin\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\le 2 \\
-1&\le 2\sin\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+1\le 3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both endpoints are attained, and every value between them is attained. Therefore, the range is $f(x)\in[-1,3]$.
Find the range of $f(x)=-3\cos\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-1$ for all real $x$.

Horizontal shifts and stretches do not change the range of cosine over all real inputs, so

$$
-1\le \cos\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\le 1.
$$

Multiplying by $-3$ reverses both inequality signs. Then subtract $1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3&\ge -3\cos\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\ge -3 \\
2&\ge -3\cos\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-1\ge -4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the smaller endpoint first gives $-4\le f(x)\le 2$. Cosine attains both $1$ and $-1$ and all values between them, so the range is $f(x)\in[-4,2]$.
Find the range of $f(x)=1-2\left(2-\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)$ for all real $x$.

First simplify the vertical transformations. The factor $-2$ multiplies both terms inside the outer parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=1-4+2\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \\
&=2\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-3.
\end{aligned}
$$

The effective vertical shift is $-3$, and the amplitude is $2$. Horizontal shifts and stretches do not change the range over all real inputs. Starting from the cosine bounds, multiply by $2$ and subtract $3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-1&\le \cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\le 1 \\
-2&\le 2\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\le 2 \\
-5&\le 2\cos\left(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-3\le -1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Cosine attains every value in $[-1,1]$, so every value between these transformed endpoints, including the endpoints, is attained. Therefore, the range is $f(x)\in[-5,-1]$.

$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=1+x+y^2$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $-1 \leq y \leq 1.$

For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(1+x+y^2\right) = 1,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(1+x+y^2\right) = 2y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z-x+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1+x+{y}^{2})-x+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2(1+2{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-\sqrt{2}y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-\sqrt{2}y)=-\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂x}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{∂z}{∂y}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{4xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot r\text{ }\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\frac{4{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}2r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}2r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta [{r}^{2}]_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =9{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\,\text{d}r \\  & =9[-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =9\cdot (-1-1) \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=- x - y$ and whose domain is the quarter-circle in the first quadrant of radius $1$ centered at $O$, as shown above. Give an exact answer.

For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}A.$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x - y)=-1,$$

and

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x - y)=-1.$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{4 y}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4 y)\cdot\sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(-1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4 y)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4 y}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 1,\ 0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4 y}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{(4(r\sin\theta))\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\int_{0}^{1}{4 r^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\left[\frac{4 r^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\left[(\left(\frac{4}{3}\right))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{\frac{4 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{3}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =\left(\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\left[- \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & =\left(\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\left[((0))-((-1))\right] \\ & =\left(\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)\cdot((0)-(-1)) \\ & =\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}$.

The point $P$ has polar coordinates $\left( 6,\dfrac{\pi}{3} \right).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P.$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta.
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
		x &= r\cos\theta\\[5pt]
		 &= 6 \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)\\[5pt]
		 &= 6 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\\[5pt]
		 &= 3
	\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
		y &= r\sin\theta\\[5pt]
		 &= 6 \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} \right)\\[5pt]
		 &= 6 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\[5pt]
		 &= 3\sqrt{3}
	\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $\left(3, 3\sqrt{3}\right).$

The closed curve $C$ is defined as $x^2+y^2 = 2.$ Find the outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C.$

We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

$$
\mathbf r(t)  
= {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( t ) \\ y ( t )\end{array} \right]}
= {\left[ \begin{array}{c}\sqrt{2} \cos   t \\ \sqrt{2} \sin   t\end{array} \right]},\qquad
t \in [0,2\pi)
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector $\mathbf r'(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $\mathbf r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{'}(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}t \\ \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation is

$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ - 1 & 0\end{array} \right]}.
$$

Rotating the vector $\mathbf r'(t)$ by $90^\circ$ clockwise, we get

$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ - 1 & 0\end{array} \right]}
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- \sqrt{2} \sin   t \\ \sqrt{2} \cos   t\end{array} \right]}
=
 {\left[ \begin{array}{c}\sqrt{2} \cos   t \\ \sqrt{2} \sin   t\end{array} \right]}.
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of $\mathbf r'(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||\mathbf r'(t)|| = \sqrt{(-\sqrt{2}\sin t)^2 + (\sqrt{2}\cos t)^2} = \sqrt{2},
$$

and since for our curve $x(t) = \sqrt{2}\cos{t}$ and $y(t) = \sqrt{2}\sin{t},$ it follows that

$$

A surface $S$ is defined, for $y>0$, by

Since $x=1$ is fixed, $y$ varies along $C$. The required slope is $f_y(1,2)$.

Holding $x$ constant, differentiate $x\ln y$ and use the quotient rule on $e^{xy}/y$. The chain rule gives $\partial(e^{xy})/\partial y=xe^{xy}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_y(x,y)&=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y(xe^{xy})-e^{xy}}{y^2}\\
 &=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{e^{xy}(xy-1)}{y^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate at $(x,y)=(1,2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m=f_y(1,2)&=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{e^2(2-1)}{4}\\
 &=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{e^2}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

As a check, the section is $g(y)=\ln y+e^y/y$. Its derivative is $g'(y)=1/y+e^y/y-e^y/y^2$, which gives the same slope at $y=2$.

\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-y)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨16{x}^{3}-8xy,\,2y-4{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =⟨16(-1)^{3}-8(-1)(1),\,2(1)-4(-1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇f(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-8,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =(-8)\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)-2\cdot \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(-1,3)$ in the direction of the vector $v=i+j.$

The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(-1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-6xy+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =(2x-6y)\,i+(2y-6x)j \\ ∇\,f(-1,3) & =(2(-1)-6(3))\,i+(2(3)-6(-1))j \\  & =-20\,i+12\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(-1,3) & =∇\,f(-1,3)\cdot u \\  & =(-20\,i+12\,j)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{-20(1)+12(1)}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=2i+j.$

The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡y+\frac{y}{x})\,i+(\frac{x}{y}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{1}{1})\,i+(\frac{1}{1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot (\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}j) \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}

In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{4})?$

At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{tan}⁡y+2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\text{ }j \\  & =-(\operatorname{tan}⁡y+4x-\frac{1}{x})i-x{sec}^{2}⁡y\text{ }j \\ -∇f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-(\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)+4\cdot 1-\frac{1}{1})i-1\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\text{ }j \\  & =-4\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $-4\,i-2\,j.$
Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ at the point $A(1,e)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-2,e).$

The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨-2,e⟩-⟨1,e⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,0⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}}}⟨-3,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-3,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(1,e):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{2x}{y}⟩ \\ ∇f(1,e) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡e,\,\frac{2(1)}{e}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\frac{2}{e}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,e) & =∇f(1,e)\cdot u \\  & =⟨2,\frac{2}{e}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,0⟩ \\  & =2(-1)+\frac{2}{e}(0) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}

In what direction does the function $f(x,y)={x}^{y}$ increase most rapidly at the point $(2,1)?$

At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{y})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{y})\,j \\  & =y{x}^{y-1}\,i+{x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(1){2}^{1-1}\,i+({2}^{1})\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,j \\  & =i+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $i+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,j.$
Consider the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}.$ What is the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(2,-1)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?

At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3})i-\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{3})j \\  & =-2x{y}^{3}\,i-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,j \\ -∇f(2,-1) & =-2(2)(-1)^{3}\,i-3(2)^{2}(-1)^{2}j \\  & =4\,i-12\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(2,-1)$ in the direction of $-∇f(2,-1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖-∇f(2,-1)‖ & =‖4\,i-12\,j‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-12)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{160} \\  & =4\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$
Find the directional derivative of the function $g(x,y)=(x^2+y)^2$ at the point $A(1,-2)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-2,2)$.

The directional derivative at a point $A$ in the direction of a nonzero vector $\mathbf v$ is

$$
D_{\mathbf u}g(A)=\nabla g(A)\cdot\mathbf u,
\qquad \mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}.
$$

The direction must be represented by a unit vector.

The direction is from $A$ towards $B$, so subtract the coordinates in that order and normalize:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf v&=\overrightarrow{AB}=\langle -2-1,2-(-2)\rangle=\langle -3,4\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf v\|&=\sqrt{(-3)^2+4^2}=5,\\
\mathbf u&=\left\langle -\frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the chain rule to both partial derivatives, then evaluate at $A$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_x(x,y)&=2(x^2+y)(2x)=4x(x^2+y),\\
g_y(x,y)&=2(x^2+y),\\
\nabla g(1,-2)&=\langle 4(1)(1-2),2(1-2)\rangle\\
&=\langle -4,-2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}g(1,-2)&=\langle -4,-2\rangle\cdot\left\langle -\frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}\right\rangle\\
&=\frac{(-4)(-3)+(-2)(4)}{5}\\
&=\frac{12-8}{5}=\frac{4}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=x^2+2xy$ at the point $(1,2)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v=2\mathbf i-\mathbf j$.

The directional derivative at a point $A$ in the direction of a nonzero vector $\mathbf v$ is

$$
D_{\mathbf u}f(A)=\nabla f(A)\cdot\mathbf u,
\qquad \mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}.
$$

The direction must be represented by a unit vector.

First, normalize the supplied direction vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf v\|&=\sqrt{2^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{5},\\
\mathbf u&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\langle 2,-1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now compute the partial derivatives and evaluate the gradient at $(1,2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2x+2y,\\
f_y(x,y)&=2x,\\
\nabla f(1,2)&=\langle 2(1)+2(2),2(1)\rangle=\langle 6,2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the dot product gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}f(1,2)&=\langle 6,2\rangle\cdot\frac{\langle 2,-1\rangle}{\sqrt{5}}\\
&=\frac{6(2)+2(-1)}{\sqrt{5}}\\
&=\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}}=2\sqrt{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Find the directional derivative of the function $h(x,y)=\dfrac{x^2+y}{x-y}$ at the point $A(2,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(-1,3)$.

The required directional derivative is {{field-1}}. Give an exact value.

The directional derivative at a point $A$ in the direction of a nonzero vector $\mathbf v$ is

$$
D_{\mathbf u}h(A)=\nabla h(A)\cdot\mathbf u,
\qquad \mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}.
$$

The direction must be represented by a unit vector.

First find the direction from $A$ towards $B$ and its unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf v&=\overrightarrow{AB}=\langle -1-2,3-1\rangle=\langle -3,2\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf v\|&=\sqrt{(-3)^2+2^2}=\sqrt{13},\\
\mathbf u&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\langle -3,2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $2-1=1\ne 0$, the function is differentiable near $A$. Use the quotient rule for each partial derivative. In the $y$ derivative, the derivative of the denominator $x-y$ is $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_x(x,y)&=\frac{2x(x-y)-(x^2+y)}{(x-y)^2},\\
h_y(x,y)&=\frac{(x-y)+(x^2+y)}{(x-y)^2},\\
h_x(2,1)&=\frac{4(1)-5}{1^2}=-1,\\
h_y(2,1)&=\frac{1+5}{1^2}=6.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the gradient at the starting point $A$, then take the dot product with the unit direction:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}h(2,1)&=\langle -1,6\rangle\cdot\frac{\langle -3,2\rangle}{\sqrt{13}}\\
&=\frac{(-1)(-3)+6(2)}{\sqrt{13}}\\
&=\frac{15}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{15\sqrt{13}}{13}.
\end{aligned}
$$
In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)=xy^2-3\ln(x+z)$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(1,2,2)$?

The point is in the domain because $x+z=3>0$. A differentiable function decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to its gradient.

Compute all three partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_x&=y^2-\frac{3}{x+z},\\
g_y&=2xy,\\
g_z&=-\frac{3}{x+z}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The logarithm contributes to the $x$ and $z$ components, but not the $y$ component. At the given point,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla g(1,2,2)&=\left\langle 2^2-\frac{3}{1+2},\,2(1)(2),\,-\frac{3}{1+2}\right\rangle\\
&=\langle 3,4,-1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Reverse every component to obtain the direction of fastest decrease:

$$
-\nabla g(1,2,2)=\langle -3,-4,1\rangle.
$$

Any positive multiple of this vector represents the same direction.
In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=x^2+xy+2y^2$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,-1)$?

A differentiable function increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient.

Compute the partial derivatives while holding the other variable constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2x+y,\\
f_y(x,y)&=x+4y.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate at the given point:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla f(1,-1)&=(2(1)+(-1))\mathbf{i}+(1+4(-1))\mathbf{j}\\
&=\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $f$ increases most rapidly in the direction of $\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$. A direction vector need not have unit length; any positive multiple points in the same direction.
In what direction does the function $h(x,y,z)=(x+y)e^{xz-y}+\ln(x+z)$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(1,1,1)$?

The point is in the domain because $x+z=2>0$. The direction of fastest decrease is opposite to the gradient.

Differentiate before substituting the point. The product rule is needed for the $x$ and $y$ partial derivatives, and the exponential requires the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
h_x&=e^{xz-y}+(x+y)z e^{xz-y}+\frac{1}{x+z},\\
h_y&=e^{xz-y}-(x+y)e^{xz-y},\\
h_z&=(x+y)x e^{xz-y}+\frac{1}{x+z}.
\end{aligned}
$$

In the $y$ partial derivative, the minus sign comes from $\partial(xz-y)/\partial y=-1$. The logarithm contributes only to the $x$ and $z$ partial derivatives.

At $(1,1,1)$, the exponential is $e^{1(1)-1}=1$ and $x+y=x+z=2$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla h(1,1,1)&=\left\langle 1+2(1)+\frac12,\,1-2,\,2(1)+\frac12\right\rangle\\
&=\left\langle \frac72,-1,\frac52\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Negate all three components:

$$
-\nabla h(1,1,1)=\left\langle -\frac72,1,-\frac52\right\rangle.
$$

Thus $h$ decreases most rapidly in this direction. Multiplying this vector by a positive number does not change its direction.
Consider the function $g(x,y)=2x^2-3y^2$. What is the rate of change of $g$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v=\langle 4,-3\rangle$?

The rate of change is the directional derivative $D_{\mathbf u}g(1,1)$, where $\mathbf u$ is the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v$.

First normalize the direction vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf v\|&=\sqrt{4^2+(-3)^2}=5,\\
\mathbf u&=\left\langle\frac45,-\frac35\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Next compute the gradient and evaluate it at the given point:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla g(x,y)&=\langle 4x,-6y\rangle,\\
\nabla g(1,1)&=\langle 4,-6\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally take the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}g(1,1)&=\nabla g(1,1)\cdot\mathbf u\\
&=4\left(\frac45\right)+(-6)\left(-\frac35\right)\\
&=\frac{16+18}{5}=\frac{34}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The positive sign means that $g$ increases in this direction.

At a point $P$, a differentiable function $f(x,y)$ has gradient $\nabla f(P)=\langle 2,-1\rangle$.

Which expression gives the rate of change of $f$ at $P$ in the direction of $\mathbf v=\langle 3,4\rangle$? You do not need to evaluate the expression.

The rate of change in a direction is the directional derivative

$$
D_{\mathbf u}f(P)=\nabla f(P)\cdot\mathbf u,
$$

where $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector in the specified direction. Since $\|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$,

$$
\mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf v}{\|\mathbf v\|}=\left\langle\frac35,\frac45\right\rangle.
$$

Thus the required expression is

$$
\langle 2,-1\rangle\cdot\left\langle\frac35,\frac45\right\rangle
=\frac{2(3)+(-1)(4)}{5}.
$$

Dividing by $5$ makes the rate a change per unit distance; using $\mathbf v$ without normalizing would give a rate for a different speed of travel.
Consider the function $f(x,y)=2xy+e^{2x-y}$. What is the signed rate of change of $f$ at the point $(1,2)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?

First compute the gradient, using the chain rule for the exponential term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x(x,y)&=2y+2e^{2x-y},\\
f_y(x,y)&=2x-e^{2x-y},\\
\nabla f(1,2)&=\langle 4+2,2-1\rangle=\langle 6,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The direction of steepest decrease is opposite to the gradient. The corresponding unit vector is

$$
\mathbf u=-\frac{\nabla f(1,2)}{\|\nabla f(1,2)\|}
=\frac{\langle-6,-1\rangle}{\sqrt{37}}.
$$

The rate in that direction is

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathbf u}f(1,2)&=\langle6,1\rangle\cdot\frac{\langle-6,-1\rangle}{\sqrt{37}}\\
&=\frac{-36-1}{\sqrt{37}}=-\sqrt{37}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, $D_{\mathbf u}f=\|\nabla f\|\cos\theta$ is smallest when $\theta=\pi$. The magnitude of the decrease is $\sqrt{37}$, but the signed rate of change is $-\sqrt{37}$.

A body of mass $3 \, \textrm{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons $(\textrm{N}).$
At time $t$ seconds, the velocity of the body is given by $v(t) =t^2- e^{t-4}$ meters per second.
Calculate the magnitude of the force at time $t=4$ seconds.

According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-{e}^{t-4}) \\  & =2t-{e}^{t-4}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the acceleration at $t=4 \, \textrm{s}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =2(4)-{e}^{4-4} \\  & =8-1 \\  & =7\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force, in Newtons, is

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =3\cdot (7) \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of the force is

$$
|F| = |21| = 21 \, \textrm{N}.
$$

A body of mass $2 \, \textrm{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t$ seconds, the position of the body is given by $s(t) = e^{3t-6} + t^2$ meters. Find the expression for the force acting on the body at time $t.$

According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,

where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{3t-6}+{t}^{2}) \\  & =3{e}^{3t-6}+2t\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{e}^{3t-6}+2t) \\  & =9{e}^{3t-6}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force acting on the body, in Newtons, is

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =2\cdot (9{e}^{3t-6}+2) \\  & =18{e}^{3t-6}+4.\end{aligned}

A body of mass $2 \, \textrm{kg}$ moves in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t\geq 0$ seconds, the velocity of the body is given by $v(t) =2t^3-12t^2-30t+5$ meters per second.
Calculate the time when the force acting on the body has a magnitude of zero.

According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration. 

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-12{t}^{2}-30t+5) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-24t-30\end{aligned}
$$

Since the mass is always positive, the force has zero magnitude when the acceleration equals zero. So, we set $a(t)=0$ and solve for $t{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{t}^{2}-24t-30 & =0 \\ {t}^{2}-4t-5 & =0 \\ (t+1)(t-5) & =0 \\ t & =-1,\,5\end{aligned}

Since $t \geq 0,$ we disregard the negative solution. 

Therefore, the force has zero magnitude when $t=5 \, \textrm{s}.$

According to Newton’s second law

The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x=x_1$ to $x=x_2$ is given by

$$
W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($\rm{J}$).

Using Newton's second law of motion, the force required to accelerate a particle of mass $3\,\rm{kg}$ at a rate of $(1 + 2x^2)\,\rm{m/s}^2$ is

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[3x+2{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =3(2)+2({2}^{3})-(3(0)+2({0}^{3})) \\  & =6+16-0 \\  & =22\,J.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

A particle $P$ of mass $6\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a force of magnitude $(8-x)\,N$ acting in the direction of increasing $x.$ Given that $x$ is measured in meters, and the particle has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at $x=1,$ calculate the velocity of the particle at $x=3.$

The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

First, we calculate the work done by the force in moving the particle from $x=1$ to $x=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(8-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[8x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =(24-\frac{9}{2})-(8-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

The particle has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at $x=1.$ So, we can find the velocity ${v}_{1}$ at $x=3$ using the work-energy principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot {6}^{2} \\ 12 & =3{v}_{1}^{2}-108 \\ 3{v}_{1} & =120 \\ {v}_{1}^{2} & =40 \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm \sqrt{40} \\ {v}_{1} & =\pm 2\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can disregard the negative solution since the velocity and acceleration of the particle are positive in the regions under consideration. 

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at $x=3$ is $2\sqrt{10}\,m/s.$

A particle $P$ of mass $8\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis from rest at the origin with an acceleration of magnitude $\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}\,{m/s}^{2},$ where the acceleration acts in the direction of increasing $x,$ and $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the particle's kinetic energy at time $t=3\,s.$

The kinetic energy of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by

$$
\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}.
$$

When the mass and velocity are measured in kilograms and meters per second, respectively, the particle's kinetic energy is measured in Joules ($J$).

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =\int \frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\ v(t) & =-\frac{1}{t+1}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
0=-\frac{1}{0+1}+C\,⟹\,C=1.
$$

Hence, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1-\frac{1}{t+1}.$ In particular, its velocity at time $t=3\,s$ is

$$
v=v(3)=1-\frac{1}{3+1}=\frac{3}{4}\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, the kinetic energy of the particle at $t=3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{KE} & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot {\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8\cdot \frac{9}{16} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

The work done by a force $F=F(x)$ in moving a particle from $x={x}_{1}$ to $x={x}_{2}$ is given by

$$
W={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

When the force and distance are measured in Newtons and meters, respectively, the work done by the force is measured in Joules ($J$).

Substituting the given values into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}({2}^{3})-({0}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}({0}^{3})) \\  & =4+\frac{8}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{20}{3}\,J.\end{aligned}

Calculate the circulation $\Gamma$ of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)=y\,\mathbf i-x\,\mathbf j$ along the closed curve $C$ traversed once according to

$$
\mathbf r(t)=3\cos t\,\mathbf i+2\sin t\,\mathbf j,\qquad 0\le t\le 2\pi.
$$

The circulation is the work done by $\mathbf F$ around the entire closed curve:

$$
\Gamma=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r
=\int_0^{2\pi}\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Along $C$, we have $x=3\cos t$ and $y=2\sin t$. Substituting these coordinates into the field and differentiating the path gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))&=2\sin t\,\mathbf i-3\cos t\,\mathbf j,\\
\mathbf r'(t)&=-3\sin t\,\mathbf i+2\cos t\,\mathbf j.
\end{aligned}
$$

Take the dot product, keeping the signs of both components:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)
&=(2\sin t)(-3\sin t)+(-3\cos t)(2\cos t)\\
&=-6\sin^2t-6\cos^2t=-6.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Gamma=\int_0^{2\pi}-6\,\mathrm dt
=\left[-6t\right]_0^{2\pi}=-12\pi.
$$

The parametrization moves counterclockwise, while the field opposes that motion, consistent with the negative result.

Calculate the circulation $\Gamma$ of the vector field

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=(x-y)\,\mathbf i+(x+y)\,\mathbf j
$$

along the ellipse $x^2+4y^2=4$, traversed once clockwise. Give an exact answer.

$\Gamma=$ {{field-1}}

The ellipse has equation

$$
\frac{x^2}{2^2}+\frac{y^2}{1^2}=1.
$$

To traverse it clockwise, use

$$
\mathbf r(t)=2\cos t\,\mathbf i-\sin t\,\mathbf j,\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi.
$$

At $(2,0)$ the velocity is $(0,-1)$, so this parametrization starts downward and has the required orientation. Along the path, $x=2\cos t$ and $y=-\sin t$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))&=(2\cos t+\sin t)\,\mathbf i+(2\cos t-\sin t)\,\mathbf j,\\
\mathbf r'(t)&=-2\sin t\,\mathbf i-\cos t\,\mathbf j.
\end{aligned}
$$

The dot product contains a term that varies along the ellipse:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t)
&=-2\sin t(2\cos t+\sin t)\\
&\quad-\cos t(2\cos t-\sin t)\\
&=-4\sin t\cos t-2\sin^2t\\
&\quad-2\cos^2t+\sin t\cos t\\
&=-2-3\sin t\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate over one complete traversal:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma&=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r\\
&=\int_0^{2\pi}(-2-3\sin t\cos t)\,\mathrm dt\\
&=\left[-2t-\frac32\sin^2t\right]_0^{2\pi}\\
&=-4\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

The varying term integrates to zero over the closed path; it cannot simply be discarded pointwise. The negative sign agrees with clockwise traversal against the rotational part of the field.

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2(1-\cos\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ (shown in blue in the picture above).

The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1-\cos\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\sin\theta.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now use the half-angle formula $1-\cos\theta =2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{2}\right)}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{2}\right)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={-4\cdot 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\theta }{2}\right))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$

$$

$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2})={t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

and

$$

x=e^t,\qquad y=e^t\cos t,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$

The indicated segment is shown below.

![Parametric curve segment with direction and parameter endpoints](images/38/38d4840253365e13b08d93e0cfcf2194e759cb95d7b7fda9ceaec3805dd5556f.png)

Choose an integral expression. Do not evaluate it.

For a parametric curve, use

$$
L=\int_a^b\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Applying the product rule to $y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}&=e^t,\\\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}&=e^t\cos t-e^t\sin t=e^t(\cos t-\sin t).\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the derivatives and the parameter limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\int_0^1\sqrt{e^{2t}+e^{2t}(\cos t-\sin t)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t\\&=\int_0^1 e^t\sqrt{1+\cos^2t+\sin^2t-2\sin t\cos t}\,\mathrm{d}t\\&=\int_0^1 e^t\sqrt{2-\sin(2t)}\,\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $y$ requires the product rule. In simplifying the speed, use $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$ and $2\sin t\cos t=\sin(2t)$. Also, $\sqrt{e^{2t}}=e^t$ because $e^t>0$. Thus the constant inside the final square root is $2$, and the cross term has a minus sign. Leave the integral unevaluated.

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=(t-1)^3+(t-1)^2,\\
y&=(t-1)^3-(t-1)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The parameter runs from $t=0$ to $t=3$.

![](images/c4/c435bdf976da9c9106c81b7620c90acd80f7f6a446703a173a3cc6a18c258757.png)

Choose an integral expression valid on the entire parameter interval. Do not evaluate the integral.

For a parametric curve, the arc length is

$$
L=\int_a^b\sqrt{[x'(t)]^2+[y'(t)]^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiate both coordinate functions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x'(t)&=3(t-1)^2+2(t-1),\\
y'(t)&=3(t-1)^2-2(t-1).
\end{aligned}
$$

Use $(A+B)^2+(A-B)^2=2A^2+2B^2$ to find the squared speed $v(t)^2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v(t)^2
 &=18(t-1)^4+8(t-1)^2\\
 &=(t-1)^2\bigl(18(t-1)^2+8\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the speed is

$$
\sqrt{[x'(t)]^2+[y'(t)]^2}
=|t-1|\sqrt{18(t-1)^2+8}.
$$

Here $t-1$ is negative for $0\leq t<1$ and positive for $1<t\leq3$. Neither $t-1$ nor $1-t$ can replace $|t-1|$ on the entire interval. Therefore,

$$
L=\int_0^3|t-1|\sqrt{18(t-1)^2+8}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

At $t=1$ both derivatives vanish, so the speed is zero there. The continuous nonnegative speed still gives the arc length across that point.

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by

$$
x=t^3+t^2,\qquad y=t^3-t^2,\qquad -2\leq t\leq-1?
$$

![](images/b3/b337ea648faf08f3ce4f904f5327193e34d3d273cf06dc1710f3170241bbc5f5.png)

Choose an integral expression. Do not evaluate the integral.

For a parametric curve, the arc length is

$$
L=\int_a^b\sqrt{[x'(t)]^2+[y'(t)]^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

First find both derivatives:

$$
x'(t)=3t^2+2t,\qquad y'(t)=3t^2-2t.
$$

The squared speed $v(t)^2$ is the sum of the squared derivatives. The cross terms cancel:

$$
\begin{aligned}
v(t)^2
 &=(3t^2+2t)^2+(3t^2-2t)^2\\
 &=9t^4+12t^3+4t^2+9t^4-12t^3+4t^2\\
 &=18t^4+8t^2=t^2(18t^2+8).
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking a square root gives $|t|\sqrt{18t^2+8}$. Since $t<0$ throughout $[-2,-1]$, we have $|t|=-t$. Therefore,

$$
L=\int_{-2}^{-1}(-t)\sqrt{18t^2+8}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

The factor $-t$ is positive on this interval. Replacing $|t|$ by $t$ would give a negative integral, which cannot be this arc length.

Find the exact arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=8 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 10 \\ y&=8 \cos{\left(t \right)} + 8 \\ t&\in\left[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{5 \pi}{12}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length is the integral of the nonnegative speed:

$$
L=\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{5 \pi}{12}}\sqrt{(x\prime(t))^2+(y\prime(t))^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiate both coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\prime(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(8 \sin{\left(t \right)} + 10\right) \\ &=8 \cos{\left(t \right)} \\ y\prime(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(8 \cos{\left(t \right)} + 8\right) \\ &=- 8 \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplify the sum of squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2&=\left(8 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)^2 \\ &\quad+\left(- 8 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)^2 \\ &=64(\cos^2 t+\sin^2 t) \\ &=64\end{aligned}
$$

On the stated interval, $8\geq0$, so taking the square root gives

$$
v(t)=\sqrt{(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2}=8.
$$

Integrating the speed gives

$$
\int 8\,\mathrm{d}t=8 t+C.
$$

Evaluate at both endpoints and subtract:

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{5 \pi}{12}}8\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\left[8 t\right]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{5 \pi}{12}} \\ &=\left(\frac{10 \pi}{3}\right)-\left(\frac{4 \pi}{3}\right) \\ &=2 \pi\end{aligned}
$$

Find the exact arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=- \frac{t^{3}}{3} + t \\ y&=t^{2} \\ t&\in\left[0,3\right].\end{aligned}
$$

$L=$
{{field-1}}

The arc length is the integral of the nonnegative speed:

$$
L=\int_{0}^{3}\sqrt{(x\prime(t))^2+(y\prime(t))^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiate both coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\prime(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- \frac{t^{3}}{3} + t\right) \\ &=1 - t^{2} \\ y\prime(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(t^{2}\right) \\ &=2 t\end{aligned}
$$

Simplify the sum of squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2&=\left(1 - t^{2}\right)^2 \\ &\quad+\left(2 t\right)^2 \\ &=t^{4} + 2 t^{2} + 1 \\ &=\left(t^{2} + 1\right)^2\end{aligned}
$$

On the stated interval, $t^{2} + 1\geq0$, so taking the square root gives

$$
v(t)=\sqrt{(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2}=t^{2} + 1.
$$

Integrating the speed gives

$$
\int t^{2} + 1\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{t^{3}}{3} + t+C.
$$

Evaluate at both endpoints and subtract:

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\int_{0}^{3}t^{2} + 1\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\left[\frac{t^{3}}{3} + t\right]_{0}^{3} \\ &=\left(12\right)-\left(0\right) \\ &=12\end{aligned}
$$

Find the exact arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=3 t + 1 \\ y&=2 t^{\frac{3}{2}} \\ t&\in\left[1,2\right].\end{aligned}

The arc length is the integral of the nonnegative speed:

$$
L=\int_{1}^{2}\sqrt{(x\prime(t))^2+(y\prime(t))^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiate both coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\prime(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(3 t + 1\right) \\ &=3 \\ y\prime(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 t^{\frac{3}{2}}\right) \\ &=3 \sqrt{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplify the sum of squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2&=\left(3\right)^2 \\ &\quad+\left(3 \sqrt{t}\right)^2 \\ &=9 t + 9 \\ &=\left(3 \sqrt{t + 1}\right)^2\end{aligned}
$$

On the stated interval, $3 \sqrt{t + 1}\geq0$, so taking the square root gives

$$
v(t)=\sqrt{(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2}=3 \sqrt{t + 1}.
$$

Integrating the speed gives

$$
\int 3 \sqrt{t + 1}\,\mathrm{d}t=2 \left(t + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}+C.
$$

Evaluate at both endpoints and subtract:

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\int_{1}^{2}3 \sqrt{t + 1}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\left[2 \left(t + 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{1}^{2} \\ &=\left(6 \sqrt{3}\right)-\left(4 \sqrt{2}\right) \\ &=- 4 \sqrt{2} + 6 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}

Find the exact arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(t \right)} \\ y&=- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)} \\ t&\in\left[0,2 \pi\right].\end{aligned}
$$

$L=$
{{field-1}}

The arc length is the integral of the nonnegative speed:

$$
L=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\sqrt{(x\prime(t))^2+(y\prime(t))^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiate both coordinates using the product rule; the opposite cross terms cancel:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\prime(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 2 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &=2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} \\ y\prime(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(- 2 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &=2 t \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplify the sum of squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2&=\left(2 t \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)^2 \\ &\quad+\left(2 t \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)^2 \\ &=4t^2(\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t) \\ &=4 t^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

On the stated interval, $2 t\geq0$, so taking the square root gives

$$
v(t)=\sqrt{(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2}=2 t.
$$

Integrating the speed gives

$$
\int 2 t\,\mathrm{d}t=t^{2}+C.
$$

Evaluate at both endpoints and subtract:

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}2 t\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\left[t^{2}\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ &=\left(4 \pi^{2}\right)-\left(0\right) \\ &=4 \pi^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the exact arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=4 t - 4 \sin{\left(t \right)} \\ y&=4 - 4 \cos{\left(t \right)} \\ t&\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length is the integral of the nonnegative speed:

$$
L=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\sqrt{(x\prime(t))^2+(y\prime(t))^2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiate both coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\prime(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(4 t - 4 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &=4 - 4 \cos{\left(t \right)} \\ y\prime(t)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(4 - 4 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &=4 \sin{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplify the sum of squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2&=\left(4 - 4 \cos{\left(t \right)}\right)^2 \\ &\quad+\left(4 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right)^2 \\ &=32\left(1-\cos(t)\right) \\ &=64\sin^2\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

On the stated interval, $\sin\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\geq0$, so taking the square root gives

$$
v(t)=\sqrt{(x\prime)^2+(y\prime)^2}=8 \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}.
$$

Integrating, including the constant chain-rule factor, gives

$$
\int 8 \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t=- 16 \cos{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}+C.
$$

Evaluate at both endpoints and subtract:

$$
\begin{aligned}L&=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}8 \sin{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\left[- 16 \cos{\left(\frac{t}{2} \right)}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &=\left(- 8 \sqrt{2}\right)-\left(-16\right) \\ &=16 - 8 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$
